title: NASA's freeze-proof battery survives minus 170°C — a step toward surviving the lunar night
excerpt: NASA's SPEARS solid-state battery prototype operated at minus 80°C and survived exposure to minus 170°C without damage — a milestone for powering rovers and habitats on the Moon.
content:
NASA has built a battery that can take the kind of cold that kills ordinary batteries — and survive to work again. In thermal vacuum testing at NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, prototype cells from the agency's SPEARS project operated at temperatures as low as minus 80 degrees Celsius (minus 112 Fahrenheit) and survived exposure to minus 170 degrees Celsius (minus 274 Fahrenheit) without damage.

The problem SPEARS is solving is simple and brutal. Traditional lithium-ion batteries, like the ones in phones and laptops, rely on liquid electrolytes. Cool one to the Moon's nighttime temperatures and the liquid freezes, potentially damaging the battery. Heat it to daytime lunar temperatures of 212 degrees Fahrenheit (100 Celsius) and it stops working until cooled. Expose the liquid to the vacuum of space and it evaporates.

SPEARS — short for Solid Power for Extreme Environment Adaptability and Resilience in Space — replaces the liquid with a solid ceramic- or polymer-based material. The project is led by NASA's Glenn Research Center, with Langley handling materials and testing and Ames preparing test boards and electronics, under the Space Technology Mission Directorate.

In the recent tests, the small prototype cells operated well from minus 60 to 80 degrees Celsius, with slightly reduced performance down to minus 80 degrees. "We proved for the first time that these cells can work down to minus 80 degrees Celsius," said Yi Lin, SPEARS testing and research lead at NASA Langley, who added that the team is confident it can improve performance and expand that range in coming years.

"Batteries have become an important part of our lives here on Earth, which enable our laptops, cell phones, power tools, and even our vehicles," said Donald Dornbusch, principal investigator for SPEARS. "We will need them on the Moon, too, and these batteries will be required to operate reliably and safely in this harsh environment."

The honest caveat: this is a milestone, not a finished product. The cells are small laboratory prototypes that have not flown in space. Even at their coldest tested exposure, minus 170 degrees, they survive but do not generate power — and nights at the lunar south pole, where NASA's Artemis program aims to go, can fall to around minus 200 degrees Celsius. NASA has also not yet published energy density, cycle life, or a flight timeline for the cells.

Still, the direction matters. A battery that needs less heating to stay alive means less mass spent on thermal management for lunar landers, habitats and rovers — and the same solid-state technology could eventually make electric-vehicle batteries safer and more reliable in extreme cold here on Earth.
